Greedy matching depends on the assignment multi-graph containing useful candidate links; if elimination removes good arms too early or leaves too many weak links, allocation quality can suffer. The abstract gives an optimality claim up to a square-root factor, but it does not show constants, implementation cost, or behavior under changing users, changing arms, strategic users, or adversarial feedback.

773.bp: The object being judged here is a short piece of speech that may be used as evidence of who said something. Modern text-to-speech and voice-conversion systems can make a voice sound like a real person, so a listener, platform, bank, or verification tool cannot safely rely on surface naturalness alone. The paper serves the larger problem of online trust: if fake audio can pass as real speech, a forged instruction, apology, threat, or identity check can travel through the web with the authority of a human voice. HierCon asks how to detect the traces left by synthetic speech when those traces are too subtle to hear directly. Its starting point is that a strong audio model already describes speech at many internal layers, from local sound patterns to broader speech structure. The paper's claim is that the useful clue is not one layer by itself, but how time steps, neighboring layers, and groups of layers fit together.
773.wh: The hard part is that real and fake speech can be close in the obvious ways. A synthetic voice may have the right speaker tone, smooth pronunciation, and plausible timing, while still carrying small artificial artifacts. A detector that checks one slice of evidence at a time can miss these artifacts because the clue may only appear as a relationship: one moment affects the next, one model layer should agree with a neighboring layer, and lower-level sound patterns should remain consistent with higher-level speech patterns. The abstract says existing detectors treat layers independently, which is like judging each page of a story without checking whether the pages follow from one another. The setting is also hard because fake audio comes from different generation techniques and recording conditions. A detector that learns the quirks of one dataset or one synthesis tool may fail when the fake is made by another tool or recorded in a different environment.
773.naive: A smart beginner would take the output of a large self-trained audio model, inspect each layer separately, and learn a weight for how useful that layer is for real-versus-fake detection. This is sensible because different layers often capture different kinds of sound evidence. It fails when the evidence is relational rather than isolated. A synthetic artifact may not be obvious in layer 8 or layer 9 alone, but may appear because layer 8 and layer 9 disagree in a way real speech rarely does. The same problem appears across time: frame-by-frame scoring can miss a fake whose individual moments sound plausible but whose sequence carries unnatural dependencies. Independent layer weighting therefore throws away the very structure HierCon is built to use.
773.ap: The core idea is to make the detector read the audio model's layers as a hierarchy instead of a pile of separate clues. HierCon uses attention, meaning learned weights that decide which pieces should influence the decision more, across three kinds of relationships named in the abstract: temporal frames, neighboring layers, and layer groups. In plain terms, it asks which moments matter, which adjacent layers support or contradict each other, and which larger bands of layers carry the strongest authenticity signal. It combines this with margin-based contrastive learning. Contrastive learning means training by comparison: descriptions of cases that should be separated are pushed apart, while useful shared structure is kept together. A margin is a required gap, so the model is not satisfied with real and fake examples being barely different. The method also encourages domain-invariant embeddings, meaning compact numeric descriptions that keep authenticity evidence while reducing dependence on a particular generator or recording condition.
773.mech: The input is an audio clip whose source is either genuine speech or speech made by a text-to-speech or voice-conversion system. First, a self-supervised audio model processes the clip. Self-supervised here means the model learned speech structure from audio itself rather than from a human label on every small sound. That model produces several layers of descriptions for the same clip, and each layer can be read across temporal frames. HierCon then does not score these layers one by one. It examines relations inside the time sequence, so a moment is interpreted partly through neighboring moments. It examines neighboring layers, so a lower or middle description can be checked against the layer beside it. It also forms layer groups, so evidence can be gathered at a coarser level than a single layer. Learned attention weights decide which frames, layer links, and layer groups should speak loudly in the final representation. During training, margin-based comparison shapes this representation: real and fake audio descriptions are arranged so the detector has a clear separation between them, not just a tiny accidental difference. The final output is a detection score or decision for whether the audio is genuine or synthetic, with the learned hierarchy supplying the evidence.
773.math: The mathematical ideas are weighted combining, comparison, hierarchy, and generalization across domains. Weighted combining is the plain core of attention: break the evidence into parts, give each part an influence number, and combine the parts after learning which ones helped past decisions. Here the parts are time frames, adjacent model layers, and groups of layers. Comparison is the core of contrastive learning: the system learns a map where cases that should be treated differently, such as real and fake speech, are separated by distance. The margin adds a practical demand: the separation must be large enough that small noise or recording changes do not erase it. Hierarchy is the idea that evidence exists at several sizes. A single frame may reveal a local artifact, neighboring layers may reveal inconsistency between sound detail and higher speech structure, and layer groups may reveal broader patterns. Domain-invariant embeddings are compact numeric descriptions designed to keep the detection-relevant signal while suppressing accidental details tied to one source domain. The tradeoff is compression versus faithfulness: the representation must ignore generator-specific clutter without discarding the subtle synthetic artifacts that prove the audio is fake.
773.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of trust, sequence reasoning, attention, and self-supervised comparison. It is close to other deepfake and misinformation papers because the practical failure is accepting synthetic media as real evidence. It is also close to sequence papers because the clue is not only what a sound frame contains, but how evidence changes over time. The connection to attention is direct: many conference papers face messy inputs where a few pieces carry more signal than the rest, and the system must learn what should count more. The connection to similarity and contrastive learning is also direct: HierCon learns a compact comparison space where real and fake speech should not collapse together. In the self-supervised and contrastive family, it is a detection branch of the same deeper problem seen in graph, retrieval, recommendation, and multimodal work: when labels or obvious rules are insufficient, construct comparisons that teach the system which differences matter.
773.ww: The mechanism should improve over the naive detector because synthetic speech artifacts are unlikely to respect every relationship that real speech respects. A generator may make each short frame sound plausible and may fool one layer of a pretrained audio model, but it still has to preserve consistency through time, across adjacent layers, and across broader layer groups. HierCon gives the detector access to those consistency checks. Attention helps because not every frame or layer is equally diagnostic; some portions may be ordinary speech, while others reveal the synthetic process. The contrastive margin helps because the training goal asks for a usable gap between real and fake descriptions, making the detector less dependent on tiny coincidences. The abstract's reported improvements over independent layer weighting fit this explanation: using relationships among layers provides information that independent weights cannot express. The claimed cross-domain generalization also fits the design, because the method tries to keep authenticity structure rather than memorize one recording condition or one generation technique.
773.po: The payoff is a stronger audio deepfake detector for a setting where fake voices are already hard to distinguish from real speech. The abstract reports results on ASVspoof 2021 DF and In-the-Wild, with equal error rates of 1.93 percent and 6.87 percent, and improvements over independent layer weighting of 36.6 percent and 22.5 percent. The practical gain is not just a better score. It is evidence that modeling temporal, neighboring-layer, and layer-group dependencies can make a detector transfer better across generation techniques and recording conditions. Attention visualizations also give some support that the model is using hierarchical structure rather than treating the audio model as a flat list of features.
773.limits: The abstract supports strong benchmark results, but it does not prove that the detector will catch every future text-to-speech or voice-conversion system. The method assumes that synthetic audio leaves detectable dependencies across time and model layers, and that these dependencies remain useful across domains. If a future generator preserves the same hierarchical relations as real speech, the signal could weaken. The domain-invariant representation also depends on learning the right distinction: it must remove recording-condition and generator-specific clutter without removing the fake-audio clue. The abstract does not detail performance under heavy noise, compression, unusual speakers, short clips, deliberate adversarial attacks, or languages and accents outside the evaluated data. It also does not show whether attention visualizations fully explain decisions or only illustrate learned weights.

774.bp: This paper is about a very practical web problem: a person wants an AI agent to do something on a website, but the action is important enough that a bad click or excessive permission could cause real harm. The abstract calls these delegated critical tasks. The object being protected is not just a password or a login session. It is the user's authority to perform particular website actions, such as the kind of task where the site should know what the agent may do, what it may not do, and under what grant from the user. Ordinary websites were built mainly for direct human interaction, where the person sees screens and presses buttons. Agentic AI changes that arrangement because the actor touching the website may be software working on the user's behalf. The paper proposes website interaction designed for that actor, with fine-grained access control so delegation can be narrower than simply handing over broad account access.
774.wh: The hard part is that delegation needs two things that pull against each other. The agent must have enough access to finish the user's task, but the website must not treat that access as a blank check. A human can notice context: this transfer is larger than expected, this setting is private, this checkout is final, this button commits something. A website receiving an agent's actions needs a machine-readable way to express similar boundaries. If it only knows that the user is logged in, the site cannot easily tell whether the agent is allowed to browse, draft, submit, approve, buy, delete, or change account settings. If it blocks agents entirely, useful automation disappears. If it allows them as ordinary users, critical tasks inherit permissions that may be too broad. The abstract says recent studies have found gaps here, mainly because websites lack access control mechanisms designed specifically for agentic AI.
774.naive: A smart beginner might say: just let the user log in, give the agent the session, and ask the agent to follow instructions carefully. That is simple, but it confuses identity with permission. Knowing who the account belongs to does not say which exact acts the agent is allowed to perform. Another beginner solution is to add a yes-or-no consent screen: allow this agent or deny it. That also fails for critical tasks because delegation is rarely all-or-nothing. The user may want the agent to fill a form but not submit it, read an order status but not cancel it, or prepare a change that still needs approval. Broad access makes mistakes and misuse costly; broad denial makes the agent useless.
774.ap: The paper's central move is to make the website itself participate in delegation, rather than treating the agent as an invisible extension of a logged-in user. It proposes a website design and implementation where the site exposes task-specific boundaries for AI agents. Fine-grained access control means the permission is divided into smaller pieces: which task, which action, which protected resource, and which critical step the agent may reach. The paper also modifies access grant protocols in an open-source authorization service, tailoring the grant process to agentic AI. In concrete terms, the agent should receive a controlled grant for the delegated task instead of inheriting every account power. The website can then check the grant when the agent interacts with task-relevant pages or operations. The abstract frames the contribution as both design and working implementation, evaluated by demonstrating the capabilities of the access-controlled website when used by agents.
774.mech: The mechanism can be understood as a gated path from user intent to website action. First, there is a user who wants to delegate a critical task to an AI agent. Second, the website must represent that task in a form its access system can check. Instead of only asking whether a logged-in account is valid, the site needs to ask a narrower question: is this agent allowed to perform this particular operation for this user under this grant? Third, an authorization service issues or manages an access grant. The abstract says the authors modify grant protocols in an open-source authorization service, so the grant is not a generic website permission but one tailored to agentic AI and delegated critical tasks. Fourth, the agent interacts with the access-controlled website. Each important step can be checked against the fine-grained grant: read permission is different from write permission, preparation is different from final commitment, and one task's permission should not silently cover another task. Finally, the site either allows the agent's requested action, blocks it, or routes it through whatever control the design requires. The output is not a new prediction or ranking. It is a safer interaction pattern in which the website can demonstrate that an agent can act while staying inside delegated boundaries.
774.math: The main mathematical idea is access control as set membership and constraint checking. A permission can be thought of as a small ticket that names an actor, an allowed operation, a resource or task, and sometimes conditions. When the agent asks to act, the system compares the requested action with the allowed set. If the requested action belongs inside the set, it can proceed; if it falls outside, it is rejected. Fine-grained access control makes the set smaller and more carefully described. That matters because a critical website task is not one indivisible blob. It has parts, and each part carries different risk. The second idea is delegation as a chain of authority. The user has authority over the account; the agent receives only a derived piece of it. The grant protocol is the rule system that records and checks that transfer. The relevant tradeoff is usefulness versus containment: make the permission too narrow and the agent cannot finish; make it too broad and the agent can cause damage beyond the intended task. There is also a systems budgeting idea: security checks must be placed at the points where actions happen, without making the website impossible to use or implement.
774.dots: This paper connects to the conference's broader agentic AI theme because many 2026 papers treat language models as workers that call tools, use websites, search, retrieve evidence, or coordinate with other agents. The nearby NANDA tutorial looks at agent registries, identity, protocols, reputation, and governance for an agentic web; this paper is a more concrete slice of that infrastructure problem, focused on website-level permission gates for delegated critical tasks. It also sits near LLM security work, such as defenses against jailbreaks and tool poisoning, because all of these papers ask what must be checked before an agent's output turns into action. The LLM agents and tool-use family in the repo describes the common pressure as building gates between language and action. Here the gate is not tool selection or cost routing. It is authorization: deciding whether the agent has the right to do this exact thing on this exact website for this exact user.
774.ww: The approach should work better than naive delegation because it moves control from a vague instruction to an enforceable boundary. A prompt that says do not exceed your authority depends on the agent interpreting and obeying language correctly every time. A website access check does not need the agent to be wise; it checks the requested action against the grant. This matters most for critical tasks, where the cost of a wrong step is higher than the cost of an ordinary browsing error. By modifying the grant protocol, the system can make delegation explicit before action occurs, rather than discovering after the fact that the agent used a power it should not have had. By designing the website for agent interaction, the protected operations can be arranged around the permission model instead of hidden behind human-only assumptions. The abstract's evaluation only claims that the resulting access-controlled website demonstrates agent capabilities, but the intuitive reason is clear: narrow, checkable grants reduce dependence on trust in the agent's self-restraint.
774.po: The payoff is a website interaction pattern where agentic AI can be used for delegated critical tasks without giving it undifferentiated account access. The paper contributes both a website design and implementation, plus changes to access grant protocols in an open-source authorization service. That combination matters because permission ideas become useful only when they are wired into the actual path by which an agent receives authority and uses a website. Grounded in the abstract, the demonstrated capability is an access-controlled website that AI agents can use while being governed by finer task boundaries.
774.limits: The abstract is short, so several important facts are not established here. It does not specify which critical tasks were tested, how many agents or users were involved, what attacks were considered, or whether the design prevents confused-agent, malicious-agent, or malicious-website behavior. The approach assumes websites are willing to redesign interaction flows and connect them to modified grant protocols. It also assumes critical tasks can be divided into clear permission units. That may be hard when actions are ambiguous, multi-step, or dependent on page context. The evaluation demonstrates capabilities, but the abstract does not prove broad deployment readiness, user comprehension, interoperability across many websites, or resistance to every misuse case.

775.bp: The ordinary object behind this tutorial is a future web where software agents, not only people and browsers, ask for help, find services, negotiate terms, and pass work to one another. A travel agent might need a payment agent, a scheduling agent, a legal-checking agent, and a supplier agent owned by different organizations. For that to work, each agent must be findable, identifiable, understandable, and worth trusting before it is allowed to act. The abstract argues that this cannot be solved by one company making a private directory. It needs shared foundations, much as the older web needed naming and communication rules before websites could become a public system. NANDA, the Network of AI Agents in a Decentralized Architecture, is presented as a way to think about those foundations across discovery, identity, protocols, pricing, reputation, markets, population behavior, governance, and coordination.
775.wh: The hard part is that an agentic web joins technical uncertainty with economic and social uncertainty. A protocol can say how two agents exchange messages, but it cannot by itself decide whether an unknown agent is honest, whether its price is fair, whether it will misuse access, or who is accountable when many agents jointly cause harm. Central control would make some decisions easier, but it would also create a bottleneck and a point of power over a web-scale population. Pure openness has the opposite failure: billions of agents could advertise incompatible abilities, fake identities, inflated reputations, or confusing terms. The abstract's comparison to DNS and HTTP matters because early architecture choices become habits. Once discovery, identity, and reputation systems harden, later agents will be shaped by those choices, including the kinds of coordination, markets, and governance they make possible.
775.naive: A smart beginner might build a large search engine for agents: every agent submits a profile, users or other agents search the directory, and the top result gets contacted through a standard message format. That handles the easiest part, finding candidates, but it fails on the deeper parts. A directory entry can lie about ability. A simple name does not prove organizational identity. A shared message format does not settle pricing, accountability, or conflict. A single directory also becomes a gatekeeper, while many independent directories fragment discovery. Another naive answer is to let reputation scores sort things out. But reputation can be gamed, can lag behind new behavior, and can hide which population or rule set produced the score.
775.ap: The core idea is to treat the agentic web as infrastructure, not as a collection of clever chatbots. NANDA organizes the problem into layers and phases. First come foundations: agents need places to register, stable identities, ways to discover one another, and common protocols for communication and resolution. Then comes the agentic economy: once agents can find and call each other, they need pricing rules, market structures, and reputation systems that make cooperation worthwhile and bad behavior costly. Finally comes agentic society: when agent populations grow large, their collective behavior needs governance, coordination rules, and ways to handle population-level effects. The paper is a lecture-style tutorial, so its central move is conceptual rather than an experiment: it gives designers a map of which infrastructure choices must be made together instead of treating discovery, trust, economics, and governance as separate afterthoughts.
775.mech: The mechanism begins with an agent that needs another agent's capability. The first requirement is discovery: some registry or registry network must let the requester find possible agents whose declared roles match the task. Next is identity: the requester needs evidence that the named agent is the one it claims to be, and that it is tied to a real organization, service, or governance domain when such a tie matters. Then comes protocol agreement: the two sides need a shared way to describe requests, permissions, expected outputs, failure cases, and handoff rules. Resolution mechanisms sit around this process, deciding how names, capabilities, or service descriptions are translated into actual endpoints and interaction choices. After contact, economic mechanisms enter. The requester may compare prices, terms, and reputation signals before choosing whom to use. The chosen agent performs or coordinates work, and the outcome can feed back into reputation or market records. At large scale, these local interactions create population dynamics: some agents become central, some disappear, some coordinate, and some may exploit weak rules. The governance layer then defines who can update standards, settle disputes, respond to abuse, and keep the ecosystem open enough for growth while bounded enough for safety.
775.math: The mathematical ideas are mostly infrastructure math: naming, networks, scoring, matching, markets, and population behavior. A registry is a structured mapping from a name or description to a reachable agent, like an address book whose entries must be checked rather than blindly trusted. A protocol is a set of allowed message shapes and state changes, which reduces ambiguity by making interactions follow known patterns. Reputation is scoring under uncertainty: many past observations are compressed into a signal about likely future behavior, while risking false confidence if the observations are biased or manipulated. Pricing and markets are matching problems with incentives: agents and requesters must be paired in ways that balance usefulness, cost, and willingness to participate. Population dynamics studies how many local decisions produce system-level behavior, such as concentration around a few trusted agents or fragmentation across incompatible communities. Governance is constraint design: deciding which actions are allowed, who can change the rules, and how conflicts are resolved. The central tradeoff is openness versus control. Too much control blocks decentralized growth; too little control makes discovery, trust, and accountability unreliable.
775.dots: This paper sits next to the repo's broader LLM agents and tool-use family, but it asks what must exist before tool-using agents can safely become web citizens. The neighboring access-control paper on delegated critical website tasks focuses on one gate: what an agent may do on a user's behalf. NANDA zooms out to the shared naming, identity, protocol, reputation, and governance substrate around such gates. It also connects to the agentic web governance position paper in the repo, which highlights access standards, business models, and multi-stakeholder coordination; NANDA treats those pressures as part of the architecture rather than only policy after the fact. The centrality paper on agentic networks is another sibling: once agents form a network, influence and information flow become measurable structure. NANDA supplies the setting in which those network questions arise, alongside recurring conference ideas about ranking, trust, markets, protocols, and decentralized coordination.
775.ww: The approach works as a conceptual foundation because it separates the agentic web into problems that have different failure modes but must interlock. Discovery without identity finds impostors. Identity without protocols proves who someone is but not how to work with them. Protocols without reputation allow communication but not trust. Reputation without economic design may reward popularity, not useful cooperation. Markets without governance can concentrate power or invite manipulation. By arranging the topic across foundations, economy, and society, NANDA makes the dependency chain visible: low-level technical rules shape later incentives, and incentives shape population behavior. The web analogy is useful because naming and communication standards became public coordination devices, not just engineering conveniences. The same reasoning fits agents: if many independent actors must coordinate across organizational boundaries, they need shared surfaces where claims can be resolved, behavior can be compared, and disputes can be handled. The tutorial's value is therefore not a single algorithmic improvement, but a way to prevent isolated design choices from becoming incompatible infrastructure.
775.po: The payoff is a design vocabulary for building agent ecosystems before they become too large to steer. Participants should leave with practical insight into registries, protocol standards, reputation systems, pricing, markets, governance, and coordination. That matters because agent infrastructure choices made early can determine whether future agents discover useful partners, communicate across organizational boundaries, and sustain cooperation without depending on one central owner. The abstract grounds the result as a lecture-style tutorial, so the benefit is conceptual readiness and research direction, not a measured speedup or accuracy gain.
775.limits: The abstract does not prove that NANDA's proposed architecture will work at web scale, resist manipulation, or produce fair markets. It says the tutorial draws on recent advances in registries, protocol standards, and resolution mechanisms, but it does not report a deployment, benchmark, user study, or formal guarantee. The argument assumes that web-native standards can be extended to autonomous agents, and that decentralized coordination can still support safety and accountability. Those assumptions may fail if agents have incompatible goals, if reputation systems are gamed, if governance excludes affected groups, or if economic incentives reward extraction rather than cooperation.

776.bp: Public language-model systems need a fast way to stop a harmful request before the model starts answering. The ordinary object here is a user prompt: a piece of text that may be a legitimate question, or may be a jailbreak, meaning wording crafted to push the model around its safety rules. Many deployed defenses look at the prompt from the outside. They try to recognize harmful intent, spot suspicious surface features, or ask a separate classifier to judge the input or output. PADD starts from a different observation: the base model already has internal signals about what parts of a prompt it is using. If a safety reminder is placed in front of the same prompt, a benign request and an adversarial request should disturb those internal focus patterns differently. The paper serves web-scale safety because it tries to make attack detection early, lightweight, and usable without retraining or changing the protected model.
776.wh: The hard part is that jailbreaks are designed to look unlike the dangerous request they carry. An attacker can change wording, add indirection, wrap the request in a role-play, or make small perturbations so a surface scanner sees something less suspicious. A post-generation defense has another problem: it spends computation producing an answer before deciding whether the answer should be blocked. A separate classifier can help, but it adds cost and may learn the same shallow clues that attackers can avoid. Modifying or fine-tuning the base model is also expensive and may not fit systems that need to protect several existing open-source models. The deeper tension is that the defense must notice intent without depending only on the prompt's outer wording. It must also be quick enough to run before generation. PADD's challenge is therefore to turn the model's own reaction to the prompt into a safety signal that separates benign from adversarial cases.
776.naive: A smart beginner would put a filter in front of the model. The filter would block prompts with dangerous words, known jailbreak phrases, or patterns that resemble earlier attacks. If that missed cases, the beginner might add an external classifier trained on benign and adversarial examples, or check the generated answer afterward. Those moves are reasonable because they match the visible evidence. They fail when the attack hides the visible evidence. Subtle prompt changes can leave the harmful instruction understandable to the model while making it unfamiliar to the filter. Output checking also pays the cost of generation and may be too late for low-latency systems. The beginner is checking the surface of the prompt, while the useful evidence may be in how the model internally reacts to safety pressure.
776.ap: PADD's central move is to create a controlled comparison for each prompt. It runs the prompt in its original form and also with a lightweight safety prefix placed before it. A prefix is just a short added instruction or reminder; here its purpose is to make the model consider safety before reading the user request. PADD then compares attention distributions, where attention means the model's internal allocation of focus across parts of the text while it is processing the prompt. It also measures attention plasticity, meaning how easily that focus pattern changes when the safety prefix is added. Instead of asking whether this prompt looks like a known attack, PADD asks whether this prompt behaves strangely when safety context is introduced. The abstract says this turns cross-prompt comparison into self-comparison: the prompt is mainly judged against its own prefixed version, not against a distant library of examples.
776.mech: The mechanism begins with one user prompt. First, PADD lets the base language model process the prompt normally and records the model's attention distribution, the pattern of how much internal focus different prompt parts receive. Second, PADD creates a second version of the same input by prepending a lightweight safety prefix. The abstract does not give the exact prefix text, so the safe claim is only that it is a short safety-oriented addition meant to nudge the model toward safety-relevant processing. Third, the same base model processes this prefixed prompt, again producing internal attention signals. Fourth, PADD compares the two runs. One signal is attention divergence: how far the focus pattern moved after the prefix was added. Another is attention plasticity: how responsive or bendable the focus pattern is under that prefix. Fifth, PADD combines these signals into a detector score. If the original and prefixed versions remain close in the way benign prompts tend to remain close, the prompt is allowed through. If the safety prefix causes a distinctive shift that separates the prompt from benign behavior, the prompt is flagged before generation. The output is a pre-generation safety decision. The important engineering point is that PADD does not fine-tune model weights, add a separate external judge, or wait for harmful content to be produced.
776.math: The main mathematical ideas are controlled comparison, distribution distance, classification, and cost-aware detection. A distribution is a set of shares that add up to a whole: in this paper, it describes how the model's internal focus is spread across prompt parts. Divergence means measuring how different two such spreads are. If the focus before and after the safety prefix is nearly the same, the distance is small; if focus moves sharply to different prompt regions, the distance is large. Plasticity adds a second view: not merely where focus moved, but how sensitive the model's focus is to the prefix. The classification problem is then to draw a boundary between benign and adversarial prompts using these composite signals. This is mathematical because the detector must compress many internal focus values into a score and choose a threshold where attacks are caught while normal users are not rejected. The tradeoff is missed attacks versus false rejection, with latency as a third constraint. PADD's self-comparison is also important: comparing a prompt to its own prefixed version controls for much of the prompt's topic and wording, so the measured change is more directly tied to how safety context alters processing.
776.dots: Within the repo's current data, this paper sits in the LLM security thread and the broader privacy, federated, and security family, where many papers ask what hidden signal crosses a boundary and how to detect it before damage occurs. PADD's boundary is the moment before generation: the system must decide whether a prompt may pass into answer production. It connects closely to RepMism, which studies a mismatch between input guardrails and the core model; PADD answers from the defender side by looking inside the model rather than trusting a separate surface reader. It also neighbors SpatialJB, where harmful meaning is hidden across layout, because both papers show that attacks can evade ordinary textual checks while remaining meaningful to the model. Prompt Forensics is another sibling: it studies safety evidence after interactions happen, while PADD tries to use internal evidence early enough to block the interaction.
776.ww: PADD should work when adversarial prompts disturb the model's safety-sensitive processing differently from normal prompts. A benign user request may change somewhat when a safety prefix is added, but the added reminder should not overturn the model's basic reading of the request. A jailbreak is different. Its wording is trying to steer the model away from ordinary safety behavior, hide intent, or make the unsafe continuation feel permissible. When the same request is prefixed with safety context, the model may redistribute focus in a more dramatic or more bendable way because the prefix conflicts with the adversarial pressure already present in the prompt. That gives PADD a signal that a surface classifier might miss. The self-comparison matters because it avoids relying only on a catalog of known attacks. The method asks, for this exact prompt, whether adding safety context exposes an unstable internal reaction. The reported low attack success rates and low false rejection rates support the idea that this internal change is more separable than raw wording alone, at least across the tested open-source models and public benchmarks.
776.po: The payoff is a practical pre-generation guard that can be attached to existing large language models. The abstract reports experiments across four mainstream open-source models and multiple public benchmarks. PADD reduces attack success rates to 0.4 to 3.0 percent while keeping false rejection rates between 0 and 5.2 percent. That means the detector is not only catching many jailbreaks; it is also, in the reported settings, rarely blocking benign prompts. Because it uses internal model signals and avoids base-model modification or fine-tuning, the promised capability is low-latency protection that can be deployed without rebuilding the model.
776.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The base model must expose attention signals, and those signals must differ consistently enough between benign and adversarial prompts after the safety prefix is added. The safety prefix must be lightweight but still strong enough to reveal the contrast. The abstract reports results on four mainstream open-source models and public benchmarks, but that does not prove transfer to closed models, future model architectures, multilingual prompts, layout-based attacks, tool-using agents, or adaptive attackers who design prompts specifically to keep attention divergence small. The abstract also does not specify the exact prefix, scoring formula, threshold choice, or latency numbers. PADD detects before generation; it does not by itself prove that every harmful output path is blocked.

777.bp: The real system here is an assistant made from several language models, where the user expects more than a fluent answer. The assistant must also notice when the question is easy, when the answer may be wrong, when its sources of knowledge disagree, and when the issue matters enough to deserve slower checking. A single language model can produce confident text even when it is uncertain, so reliability becomes partly a self-monitoring problem: the system needs a way to look at its own answer process before deciding how to answer. This paper implements a metacognition setup for an ensemble of models. Metacognition means thinking about one's own thinking; in this system it means measuring signs of confidence, conflict, fit to past experience, and importance, then using those measurements to choose either fast answering or a more deliberate multi-model process.
777.wh: The hard part is that uncertainty in language models is not one thing. A model may be unsure because the query is outside what it knows, because different models produce incompatible answers, because the problem is important enough that a casual answer is risky, or because the system's own correctness checks look weak. Treating all questions the same wastes effort on simple cases and under-invests in difficult ones. Treating uncertainty as a single confidence number also loses important distinctions: a question can feel familiar but still contain conflict, or it can be answerable but high-stakes. The abstract says the system must monitor five dimensions and then control processing, which means it has to turn soft signs of self-awareness into operational decisions: who should respond, whether deliberation is needed, and which model should play which role.
777.naive: A smart beginner might send every user query to one strong model and ask it to answer plus state its confidence. If the confidence is low, the system could ask another model or make the first model reason longer. This fails because stated confidence is not the same as knowing whether the answer process is trustworthy. The model may not notice a hidden knowledge conflict, may overrate familiar-looking questions, or may underrate problem importance. Another naive fix is to always use a large ensemble for every query. That improves checking in some cases, but it spends extra computation even when the query is simple and still needs a rule for organizing disagreement.
777.ap: The paper's central move is to make self-monitoring explicit. Instead of hoping that a model's final answer carries enough warning signs, the system computes a Metacognitive State Vector, or MSV, for the ensemble nodes. A vector is just an ordered list of measurements; here the measurements are emotional response, correctness evaluation, experiential match, conflicting information, and problem importance. These values become both a dashboard for awareness and a control signal for action. When the MSV pattern suggests a simple or low-conflict query, the system can use System 1 processing, meaning a fast single-node or multi-node path. When the values suggest complexity or conflict, the system switches to System 2 processing, meaning slower deliberation across multiple nodes with roles such as Domain Expert, Critic, Evaluator, Synthesizer, and Generalist.
777.mech: The input is a user query sent to an ensemble of language-model nodes. The system first evaluates the query and the model states through the five MSV dimensions named in the abstract. Emotional response is a signal about how the system reacts to the query; correctness evaluation asks whether the emerging answer appears right; experiential match asks whether the query resembles situations the system can handle; conflicting information records disagreement or tension; problem importance estimates whether the answer deserves extra care. Those measurements produce a state vector for monitoring. Next, the same state values are used for control. If the query looks simple enough, the system routes it to a fast System 1 path, either through one node or a small multi-node route. If the query looks complex, conflicted, or important, it routes the work to System 2. In that slower mode, graph-theoretic algorithms treat ensemble nodes and roles as parts of a connected assignment problem. The system assigns nodes to specialized roles according to their measured states: one node may act as a domain expert, another as a critic, another as an evaluator, another as a synthesizer, and another as a generalist. The output is not only an answer path but also visible indicators, such as real-time radar charts and decision markers in the proof-of-concept demo.
777.math: The main mathematical object is the Metacognitive State Vector. A vector is useful because the system is measuring several different properties at once instead of squeezing them into one vague confidence score. The tradeoff is detail versus simplicity: five measurements preserve more reasons for caution, but the system must then decide how their pattern should control action. The second mathematical idea is routing as a decision rule. Routing means choosing a path for work: fast System 1 when the measured state looks safe enough, or deliberate System 2 when the state suggests complexity. The third idea is graph reasoning. A graph is a collection of points and links; here the points can be understood as ensemble nodes and specialized roles, while the links encode possible assignments or coordination paths. Graph algorithms fit because System 2 is not just asking more models randomly. It is arranging different responsibilities among connected participants. The system also uses scoring: correctness evaluation, conflict, match, and importance become quantities that can be compared. The risk is false precision. A number can make uncertainty look cleaner than it is, so the usefulness depends on whether the MSV measurements actually correspond to meaningful signs of model reliability.
777.dots: This paper sits near several recurring conference ideas. It connects to language-model reliability because it addresses a basic failure of fluent assistants: they may answer even when they should pause, check, or admit conflict. It connects to ranking and routing because the system must choose among processing modes and role assignments, not merely generate text. It connects to graph reasoning because the deliberate mode organizes ensemble nodes through graph-theoretic assignment rather than treating models as an unordered crowd. It also touches recommendation-like decision making: given a query and several possible workers or roles, the system recommends a processing path. The neighboring idea is uncertainty estimation, but the paper's version is broader than a single probability of being wrong. It breaks uncertainty into conflict, importance, experience match, and correctness signals so the system can decide how much thinking the situation deserves.
777.ww: The mechanism should help because it separates two jobs that are often mixed together: producing an answer and deciding how much trust the answer process deserves. A naive model answers first and explains confidence afterward. This system measures metacognitive state before and during routing, so uncertainty can change the process itself. If there is little conflict and the query matches what the system appears able to handle, a fast path saves effort. If conflict or importance is high, the system creates a slower structure where different nodes are assigned different duties. A critic can search for weaknesses, an evaluator can judge quality, and a synthesizer can combine outputs. That division matters because disagreement is more useful when it is organized. The MSV also gives users and developers visible evidence about why a query took one route rather than another, which can make the system's behavior easier to inspect.
777.po: The payoff claimed by the abstract is a working proof of concept for metacognitive self-awareness and self-regulation in language-model ensembles. The demo lets users explore how different query types trigger different modes, moving between fast System 1 processing and deliberate System 2 processing. It also visualizes the process with radar charts and decision indicators, so the routing is not hidden inside a black box. In practical terms, the system buys a way to spend more reasoning effort on queries that appear complex, conflicted, or important, while keeping simpler queries faster.
777.limits: The abstract describes a proof-of-concept demo with illustrative examples, so it does not prove broad reliability in deployed settings. The approach assumes that the five MSV dimensions can be measured well enough to guide decisions; if those measurements are noisy or poorly calibrated, the routing may become misleading. It also assumes that graph-based role assignment improves deliberation rather than merely adding ceremony. The abstract does not report large-scale user studies, failure rates, or comparisons against simpler ensemble baselines. It shows feasibility and visualization, not yet a guarantee that the system truly knows when it is outside its expertise.

778.bp: Many search and recommendation systems first turn each item into a point described by numbers, then answer a request by finding nearby points. This works well when the request has one center: this query, this product, this image, or this user profile. The paper starts from the fact that many real requests are not centered on one example. A shopper may want items close to several favorites at once. A recommendation system may need items that satisfy a group of interests, or items that match at least one of several acceptable tastes. Traditional approximate nearest neighbor search, meaning fast search for nearly closest items without scanning everything, is built around one reference vector. This paper asks what search should mean when the query contains several reference vectors, and how to make that practical on the graph indexes already used for ordinary nearest neighbor search.
778.wh: The hard part is that a single-reference search has one simple question: which stored points are closest to this query point? With several reference points, closeness becomes a rule choice before it becomes an engineering problem. Similar to all references is different from similar to any reference. A candidate that is excellent for one reference and terrible for another may be perfect for an any-style request and poor for an all-style request. The system also has to return the top k candidates, so it needs an ordering over stored vectors, not just a yes-or-no test. A brute force answer would compare every stored vector with every reference vector and then sort the whole dataset, but large machine learning collections are too big for that. The challenge is to define the right distance measures and then search them efficiently without rebuilding the indexing world from scratch.
778.naive: A smart beginner would run ordinary nearest neighbor search once for each reference vector, then combine the result lists. For an all-style query, they might intersect the lists and keep candidates appearing near every reference. For an any-style query, they might merge the lists and remove duplicates. This breaks because approximate search lists are incomplete by design, so a good candidate may be missing from one early list even though it should rank well under the multi-reference rule. It also wastes work: each reference starts a separate search even though the final decision depends on their joint score. Most importantly, list intersection and merging do not by themselves define the exact ranking that the paper wants to approximate.
778.ap: The paper's core move is to make multi-reference search a first-class nearest neighbor problem instead of a collection of single-reference searches. It introduces all/any-k search. In all-k search, a returned vector should be similar to all of the reference vectors in the query. In any-k search, a returned vector should be similar to at least one of them. The authors first propose distance metrics for the exact version of these problems, so every stored vector can be ranked according to the intended meaning of all or any. Then they design approximate search algorithms that follow those metrics on graph indexes originally built for traditional single-reference approximate nearest neighbor search. Finally, they add two-stage algorithms to improve search performance, using a first pass to find promising regions and a second pass to refine the answer.
778.mech: The input is a dataset of vectors, a graph index over those vectors, and a query containing multiple reference vectors. The graph index can be pictured as a road map among stored points: each point links to nearby points, so search can move through neighbors instead of checking the entire dataset. First, the method decides which multi-reference rule is being asked for. For all-k, the score must express how well a candidate stays close to every reference. For any-k, the score must express whether the candidate is close to at least one reference. Second, the proposed distance metric turns that rule into an ordering over dataset vectors, which says which candidates would be best if exact search were affordable. Third, the approximate algorithm searches the existing graph according to that ordering. It visits candidate nodes, evaluates them against the multiple reference vectors, compares their multi-reference scores, and follows graph links toward nodes that appear more promising under the all or any rule. Fourth, the algorithm maintains the best candidates found so far until it can return the top k approximate answers. The two-stage version adds a performance layer: one stage gathers a useful candidate set or search region, and another stage applies more focused scoring or traversal to produce the final ranked results.
778.math: The main mathematical idea is distance, but not distance as a single fixed formula. Distance here means a rule for turning several comparisons into one order. With one reference vector, each stored vector has one closeness value. With several reference vectors, each stored vector has a small collection of closeness values, one per reference, and the method must combine them according to the user's intent. All-style search needs a measure that punishes being far from one reference even if the candidate is close to another, because the candidate is supposed to satisfy every reference. Any-style search needs a measure that rewards being close to at least one reference, because satisfying one reference is enough. Ranking is the second idea: the metric is useful only because it lets the system sort candidates and choose the top k. Graph search is the third idea. The graph links encode local nearness, so moving through neighbors is a cheap way to explore a huge vector collection. The proof claim in the abstract matters because adapting a graph built for ordinary nearest neighbor search is not automatically valid for these new metrics. The tradeoff is speed versus exactness: the system accepts approximate answers, but it tries to approximate the right multi-reference ordering rather than a pile of single-reference lists.
778.dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of similarity, ranking, recommendation, retrieval, graph reasoning, and efficiency. It belongs to similarity because it asks what kind of closeness should be trusted when a request has several centers rather than one. It belongs to ranking because the goal is not merely to find acceptable matches, but to order the dataset so the best k candidates rise to the top. It connects to recommender systems because the abstract names recommendation as a common use of approximate nearest neighbor search, and multi-reference queries naturally match recommendation moments involving several interests, examples, or users. It connects to information retrieval because it broadens the shape of a query: a request can be a set of reference objects, not a single point. It also connects to graph and efficiency papers because the proposed algorithms run on graph indexes designed for traditional approximate search, preserving the practical shortcut of walking through nearby nodes instead of scanning all vectors.
778.ww: The approach should work better than the naive plan because it aligns the search procedure with the actual question. If the user asks for items close to all references, searching each reference separately and intersecting results treats each single-reference ranking as independent, even though the final answer depends on the worst or joint behavior across references. If the user asks for items close to any reference, independent list merging can overvalue whichever single search happened to return many candidates and can miss candidates because each approximate list is only partial. By defining the multi-reference distance first, the paper gives every candidate one task-specific score. The graph traversal can then spend its limited search steps on nodes that are promising under that score. Reusing traditional graph indexes helps because those graphs already capture local neighborhoods in the vector dataset. If nearby nodes tend to have related distances to the references, walking from promising nodes to their neighbors can find good multi-reference candidates without an exhaustive scan. The two-stage design further helps by separating broad candidate discovery from sharper final selection.
778.po: The payoff is a more expressive form of fast vector search. Systems are no longer limited to asking for neighbors of one reference vector. They can ask for vectors similar to all references in a query or similar to any reference in a query, while still using graph indexes made for traditional approximate nearest neighbor search. The abstract says the authors define exact ranking metrics, prove that their algorithms search according to those metrics on existing graph indexes, and validate efficiency and effectiveness on real-world datasets against existing approaches. In practical terms, the paper expands what recommendation and other machine learning applications can ask from a nearest neighbor search layer.
778.limits: The method assumes that the vector representation already makes meaningful items near one another. If the vectors place wrong things close together, multi-reference search will combine bad comparisons more carefully, but it will not fix the representation. It also assumes the proposed all and any distance metrics match the application's intent; some real group or multi-interest queries may need richer rules than all references or any reference. The abstract does not specify dataset types, index details, parameter sensitivity, or how performance changes as the number of reference vectors grows. Approximate graph search can miss true top candidates, so the proof and experiments matter within the stated metric and index setting, not as a guarantee for every deployment.

779.bp: The paper is about a moderation system that must judge whether a social-media post is misleading when the warning signs are small, scattered, and dependent on context. A false post may not look strange in every way. Its wording, source, timing, image, or relation to other claims may each contain only a faint clue. The practical need is a detector that can notice those faint clues before they are buried under the much larger amount of ordinary true material around them. PAMAS uses several language-model agents, meaning several model-driven workers that can inspect evidence and report conclusions, because one all-purpose judge can miss details that matter. The paper's theme is misinformation, but the deeper problem is selective attention under overload: how to make a group of reasoning workers look at the right slices of evidence, exchange what they find, and produce one final judgment without letting the loudest normal pattern dominate.
779.wh: The hard part is that social media contains far more normal-looking and truthful material than clear deceptive clues. If every agent sees the full input, each agent is tempted to explain the case using the strongest surface pattern, which is often the ordinary content rather than the suspicious residue. Communication can make this worse. When agents share broad summaries with one another, the same dominant interpretation can echo through the group, so cooperation becomes a way to amplify bias instead of a way to discover missed evidence. The abstract calls this information drowning: the important signal is not absent, but it is weak compared with the volume of surrounding content. A detector therefore has to solve two problems at once. It must widen coverage so different kinds of cues are inspected, and it must keep those views diverse enough that rare anomaly cues are not averaged away before the final decision.
779.naive: A smart beginner would give the whole post and all available context to several agents, ask each one whether it is misinformation, then vote or average their answers. That sounds reasonable because more agents should mean more checking. It fails when the agents all look at the same dominant evidence. If the post is mostly plausible and only a small part is deceptive, full access can steer every agent toward the plausible part. A second beginner move is to let agents discuss freely, but the abstract says inter-agent communication can further amplify the bias. The group may become more confident in the easy majority pattern while the sparse deceptive cue remains underexamined.
779.ap: PAMAS makes the group less flat. Instead of treating every agent as another copy of the same judge, it assigns roles and controls what each role sees. Auditors examine specialized feature subsets, so each auditor is responsible for catching anomaly cues in a narrower view of the case. Coordinators then combine auditor perspectives in a way meant to increase coverage while preserving diversity, so one strong but ordinary perspective does not erase the weaker ones. A final Decision-Maker has full contextual access and evolving memory, then synthesizes the subordinate insights into the final judgment. The paper also adds self-adaptive mechanisms for dynamic topology optimization and routing-based inference. In plain terms, the system can adjust who communicates with whom and which reasoning path is used, so collaboration is not always forced through the same expensive pattern.
779.mech: The input is a social-media case and its available context, represented through multiple kinds of features rather than one undivided bundle. PAMAS first divides the inspection labor among Auditors. Each Auditor receives a specialized subset of evidence and looks for anomaly cues inside that slice. The output from this level is not the final misinformation label; it is a set of partial observations, each shaped by a particular perspective. Next, Coordinators gather these partial observations. Their job is to aggregate, meaning to combine reports into a smaller and more useful form, while maintaining diversity. That matters because coverage and diversity pull against each other: combining reports too aggressively saves effort but can erase rare clues, while keeping every report separate preserves detail but can drown the next stage. The Decision-Maker then sees the full context plus the coordinated insights. Its evolving memory lets it carry forward useful patterns from earlier reasoning steps or cases, as described in the abstract, while still making the final call from the current evidence. Finally, the self-adaptive part changes the collaboration structure and routes inference through selected paths. The output is a misinformation judgment produced after specialized cue finding, hierarchical combination, and final synthesis.
779.math: The main mathematical idea is weighted aggregation under scarcity. Aggregation means many separate reports must become one decision. The danger is that a plain average gives the largest mass of evidence the largest voice, even when the truth depends on a small anomaly. PAMAS therefore treats perspectives as objects to be preserved and combined, not as interchangeable votes. A second idea is anomaly detection, which asks whether a detail fails to fit the expected pattern. Here the anomaly is a weak deceptive cue hidden among truthful content. The math must compare each specialized slice against what looks ordinary in that slice, because a clue can be small globally but sharp locally. A third idea is routing and topology choice. A topology is the communication map among agents; routing decides which path information follows through that map. Dynamic topology optimization means defining a cost, such as unnecessary communication or missed useful coverage, and changing the agent connections to reduce that cost. The tradeoffs are explicit: breadth versus noise, diversity versus agreement, speed versus completeness, and local suspicious detail versus global context. The paper's math fits because misinformation detection is not only classification; it is controlled evidence movement.
779.dots: This paper connects to the conference's recurring work on misinformation, anomaly detection, language-model agents, ranking, and efficient decision systems. It is close to fake-news papers that retrieve outside evidence or inspect multimodal cues, because all of them face the same deeper problem: the false part of a claim is often not obvious from one surface signal. It also belongs near anomaly-detection work, where the goal is to notice a rare pattern without treating every rare pattern as harmful. PAMAS differs by putting the anomaly search inside a group of language-model agents and then managing the group's communication. The routing and topology pieces connect it to systems papers that save time and computation by sending only useful information along selected paths. Its perspective aggregation also echoes recommendation and ranking ideas: decide which evidence deserves influence, whose view should count, and how to combine many partial signals into one ordered judgment.
779.ww: The mechanism should help because it changes where evidence has a chance to become visible. In the naive full-access setup, every agent sees the same large pile and may settle on the same broad explanation. In PAMAS, an Auditor looking only at a specialized feature subset has less irrelevant material competing for its attention, so a weak cue can become a strong cue within that narrower view. Coordinators then keep the useful middle ground: they reduce the number of reports the final stage must read, but they are designed to maintain different perspectives rather than collapse everything into one majority opinion. The Decision-Maker restores global context at the end, which is important because an isolated anomaly is not enough; it must be judged against the full post and context. The adaptive communication structure helps for efficiency because not every case needs the same amount of agent interaction. Easy cases can use shorter routes, while harder cases can preserve more collaborative checking.
779.po: The payoff is a misinformation detector built for cases where deceptive cues are sparse and weak. According to the repo data and the full local abstract, PAMAS reports stronger accuracy and efficiency on multiple benchmark datasets by using hierarchical perspective aggregation, evolving memory, dynamic topology optimization, and routing-based inference. In practical terms, it buys a more disciplined way to use language-model agents: not simply more agents talking, but agents organized so specialized observations can survive long enough to affect the final decision. That makes the system more plausible for larger-scale misinformation detection, where communication cost and missed rare cues both matter.
779.limits: The abstract does not prove that PAMAS will work on every platform, language, event type, or coordinated misinformation campaign. It assumes that useful anomaly cues exist inside the chosen feature subsets and that Auditors can detect them well enough to pass them upward. It also assumes the aggregation design really preserves diversity rather than just renaming another averaging step. Evolving memory can help if past patterns remain relevant, but it can mislead when misinformation tactics change. Dynamic topology and routing improve efficiency only if the routing choices do not skip the agent that would have seen the decisive weak cue. The abstract reports experiments, but not deployment evidence under live adversarial pressure.
